findings.summary: Every page title after page 1 names a chapter whose material was already taught on the preceding page, so the running headers point a learner at the wrong content — worst at pages 6 and 7, which contain none of the topic their title promises.
findings.evidence: Page 6 is titled "Containment and Existence" but its blocks are `"`||` on objects is a shallow merge, right side wins"`, `"jsonb_set"`, `"What Updates Cost"`, `"Concurrency"`; page 7 is titled "Mutating Documents" but opens with `"Unnest A Document"` / `"`jsonb_each(v)` → (key text, value jsonb)"`. Containment was actually taught on pages 4–5 and mutation on pages 5–6.
findings.fix: Re-title each page from the material it actually carries and mark spill pages consistently: page 3 → "Extraction: Arrows, Paths, Subscripts", page 4 → "Containment and Existence", page 5/6 → "Mutating Documents" with `cont:true` on the second, page 7/8 → "Documents to Rows and Back", page 9 → "SQL/JSON Path Queries".

findings.summary: The Unicode-escape restrictions described apply only to `jsonb`, not to both types as claimed.
findings.evidence: "Neither type accepts `\u0000` inside strings" and "Server encoding must represent every `\uXXXX` escape"
findings.fix: Rewrite as jsonb-only: "`jsonb` rejects `\u0000` and any `\uXXXX` the server encoding cannot represent; `json` accepts them on input (checked only for syntactic correctness) and errors later, when a processing function or a cast to text converts the escape." Per the PostgreSQL docs: "Unicode escapes are allowed regardless of the database encoding... However, the input function for the jsonb is stricter... The jsonb type also rejects \u0000".

findings.summary: The jsonpath filter example uses `is unknown` without the parenthesized predicate the grammar requires, so it is a syntax error.
findings.evidence: "'$ ? (exists(@.addr) && !(@.x is unknown))'"
findings.fix: `is unknown` takes a parenthesized boolean predicate, not a path — the docs' form is `'$[*] ? ((@ > 0) is unknown)'`. Replace the line with a valid example, e.g. `'$ ? (exists(@.addr) && !((@.x > 0) is unknown))'`.

findings.summary: The described JSON parse error reports a token and a line, not a byte position.
findings.evidence: "-- bad text: invalid input syntax for", "-- type json, with a byte position"
findings.fix: Change the comment to reflect the real message shape: `ERROR: invalid input syntax for type json / DETAIL: Token "}" is invalid. / CONTEXT: JSON data, line 1: ...` — i.e. the offending token plus a line and excerpt, no byte offset.

findings.summary: "Subscript" is used to mean the integer argument of `->` one page before subscripting is introduced as a separate feature, so the two readings collide.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Wrong shape is quiet too: integer subscript on an object yields NULL"; page 4 then introduces "Subscripting" as `data['user']['city']`, a distinct PG 14+ syntax.
findings.fix: Reword the page 3 bullet to the operator it is actually about — "an integer argument to `->` on an object yields NULL" — and reserve "subscript" for the `data['k']` form on page 4.

findings.summary: The subscripting section tells the reader to reach for GIN and expression indexes, neither of which is defined in this part, and the syllabus's forward pointer was dropped.
findings.evidence: "None of these operators are GIN-indexable on their own" / "`data->>'x' = 'y'` needs an expression index or a rewrite to `@>`". The syllabus bullet ends "(see Ch. 8-9)"; the page carries no such cross-reference.
findings.fix: Restore the pointer on both bullets, e.g. "— see the GIN and expression-index pages later in this handbook", so the unexplained terms read as a forward promise rather than assumed knowledge.

findings.summary: The absent-key vs JSON-null callout prescribes the `?` operator a full page before `?` is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 4 callout "Tell Them Apart": "Use `data ? 'k'` for existence, or `jsonb_typeof(data->'k')`." The "Existence Operators" table defining `?` first appears on page 5.
findings.fix: Lead with the already-taught tool — "Use `jsonb_typeof(data->'k')`, or the `?` operator on the next page" — or move the callout to page 5 after `?` is defined.

findings.summary: A deep-existence code block hands the learner working jsonpath syntax four pages before jsonpath is introduced.
findings.evidence: "WHERE data @? '$.**.email'        -- deep" on page 5; `jsonpath`, `$`, `.**` and `@?` are not introduced until pages 8–9 ("`jsonpath` is its own type, added in PG 12").
findings.fix: Keep the `#>` + `?` line as the taught answer and reduce the jsonpath line to a labelled forward pointer ("or jsonpath `@?` — see the jsonpath pages"), without the unexplained `$.**` syntax.

findings.summary: The acronym HOT is used as the condition that decides index write cost but is never expanded or defined.
findings.evidence: "Every index on the table is touched unless the update qualifies as HOT".
findings.fix: Expand it inline: "unless the update qualifies as HOT (heap-only tuple: no indexed column changed and the new version fits on the same page, so no index entry is written)".
